fixes.explanation: The law of Moses is a well-known name, but it doesn't show up in these verses. Paul says he didn't act in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God. So the answer is grace. The law of Moses isn't part of this boast.

Paul says the opposite here. He writes, “…we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand.” So what he writes is within their ability to read and understand. He even hopes they will understand completely.

That's right, friend. Paul says, “…we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand.” What he writes, they can read and understand. I respect that, because my recipes have been called a lot of things, and readable is not always one of them.

Galatia isn't on this route, friend. Paul names two places: Macedonia on the way, and Judea at the end. He wanted the Corinthians to help him on his way to Judea. I've been lost in the back of a junk drawer, and even I can follow this map.

Most sounds pretty generous, and it's still a step short of what Paul writes. He says all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ. The word is all, not most. That's why he says our “Amen” is spoken through Him to the glory of God.

True! Paul writes that God “…placed His seal on us…” Right next to that, he says God anointed them and put His Spirit in their hearts. That's three things God did, stacked one right after another, and Paul isn't slowing down.

His Spirit, baker. Paul says God “…put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.” The Spirit is the pledge, a guarantee of what is to come. The Spirit is in their hearts now, and what is to come is still ahead.

His fear isn't what Paul says is placed in the heart here. He writes that God “…put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.” The Spirit is the pledge, a guarantee of what is to come. So the Spirit is the one to hold on to.

Those he grieved, friend. Paul asks, if he grieves the Corinthians, who is left to cheer him but those whom he has grieved? So the ones he names are the very people he would have grieved. Their joy matters to him.

Anger isn't what Paul says. He writes that he wrote through many tears out of great distress and anguish of heart, “…not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” He names his purpose himself, and the purpose is love.

Paul says it the other way around. He says if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved Paul but all of them, to some degree, not to overstate it. So the grief he names belongs to all the Corinthians. That makes this one False.

Forgive and comfort him, baker. Paul says, “…you ought to forgive and comfort him…” He says the punishment imposed by the majority is sufficient. So mercy is what comes next, so that the man will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Obedient, baker. Paul says his purpose in writing was to see if they would “…stand the test and be obedient in everything.” So he wrote to see how they would do. And I think he's hoping they pass.

Christ, friend. Paul says that if he has forgiven anything, he has forgiven it in the presence of Christ for their sake. So Christ is the one in whose presence he forgives. The church is who it's for.

Satan, baker. Paul says he forgives in order that Satan should not outwit them, and adds, “…we are not unaware of his schemes.” So his forgiving is tied to Satan not outwitting them. It's a serious line, and Paul says it plainly.
